SIRT1 expression sensitized ALL to panobinostat through activating mitochondrial activity and the mitochondria-related apoptosis pathway. Visual Abstract Abstract Epigenetic alterations, including histone acetylation, contribute to the malignant transformation of hematopoietic cells and disease progression, as well as the emergence of chemotherapy resistance. Targeting histone acetylation provides new strategies for the treatment of cancers. As a pan-histone deacetylase inhibitor, panobinostat has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of multiple myeloma and has shown promising antileukemia effects in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). However, the underlying drug resistance mechanism in ALL remains largely unknown. Using genome-wide Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas)9 (CRISPR/Cas9) screening, we identified mitochondrial activity as the driver of panobinostat resistance in ALL. Mechanistically, ectopic SIRT1 expression activated mitochondrial activity and sensitized ALL to panobinostat through activating mitochondria-related apoptosis pathway. Meanwhile, the transcription level of SIRT1 was significantly associated with panobinostat sensitivity across diverse tumor types and thus could be a potential biomarker of panobinostat response in cancers. Our data suggest that patients with higher SIRT1 expression in cancer cells might benefit from panobinostat treatment, supporting the implementation of combinatorial therapy with SIRT1 or mitochondrial activators to overcome panobinostat resistance. Introduction Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most prevalent malignant disease in children. 1 Long-term prognosis in children with ALL has dramatically improved in recent decades, with the 5-year event-free survival rate approaching 90%. 2 The success of ALL treatment is mainly attributed to refinement of therapy based on a better understanding of clinical and biological characteristics of the disease. However, small subsets of patients who experienced drug resistance would relapse with a dismal prognosis, and thus novel treatment strategies are needed. 3 Advances in high-throughput multi-omics have further provided insights into the underlying molecular mechanisms of ALL and drug resistance. Growing evidence has shown that many genetic and epigenetic factors are associated with drug response and ALL relapse. 4,5 In recent years, novel epigenetic modulation agents (eg, azacytidine, decitabine, and vorinostat) are promising in clinical efficacy. 6-10 For example, DNA methyltransferase inhibitors (eg, 5-azacitidine), which can remove promoter hypermethylation in tumor cells and restore the gene expression signature, have achieved significant progress in the treatment of myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome. 6,7 Furthermore, histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors such as vorinostat and panobinostat have been approved in clinical use for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma. 9-11 HDACs regulate chromatin structure and function by removing acetyl residues from the core histones. 5 Deregulation of HDAC activity has been closely implicated in the silencing of differentiation and tumor suppressor genes, resulting in the promotion of oncogenesis, particularly leukemia. 12,13 Interestingly, targeting HADCs has demonstrated potent antitumor activity in preclinical models and promising clinical efficacy in patients with cancer (eg, multiple myeloma and T-cell lymphoma). 14,15 Panobinostat is a pan-HDAC inhibitor and has exerted promising cytotoxic activities against different cancer cells, including ALL. 16-19 Garrido Castro et al 18 demonstrated that panobinostat exerted antileukemia activity in a B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) xenograft mouse model. Meanwhile, many clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate its therapeutic value against ALL. 20,21 Although panobinostat is a promising antileukemia agent, the efforts to maximize its clinical benefit for acute leukemia will not succeed unless more details are known about its subtype specificity, functional mechanisms, and resistance mechanisms. In the present study, we performed a genome-wide Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas)9 (CRISPR/Cas9) loss-of-function screening in B-ALL cells in the presence or absence of panobinostat to discover the molecule mechanism of its action and resistance.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Panobinostat resistance and sensitivity in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and other cancers; modulating panobinostat sensitivity and response to other HDAC inhibitors.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Panobinostat resistance in ALL is driven by mitochondrial activity, where panobinostat abrogates mitochondrial activity, leading to an inactive OXPHOS state and allowing ALL cells to escape drug-induced apoptosis. Defects in mitochondrial function contribute significantly to this resistance. Conversely, ectopic SIRT1 expression or activation enhances mitochondrial activity and the mitochondria-related apoptosis pathway, sensitizing ALL cells to panobinostat. This involves SIRT1 deacetylating PGC1-1α, which activates downstream genes for mitochondrial replication and respiration. The SIRT1-mitochondria-PMAIP1 axis is crucial for panobinostat sensitivity, increasing expression of proapoptotic proteins like PMAIP1 and cleaved PARP. Genes involved in acetylation modification (SIRT1, ACLY, CREBBP, KAT7) are also implicated, consistent with panobinostat's role as a pan-HDAC inhibitor. Loss of function of BAK1 and PMAIP1 confers apoptosis resistance by disrupting mitochondria-dependent apoptosis pathways. Defects in the p53 signaling pathway and enrichment for mitochondrial-related processes (thermogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial translation) also contribute to resistance.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Panobinostat was frequently used at 10 nM for treatment in various experiments. Rosiglitazone was used at 31.25 μM. Gradient concentrations of panobinostat were used in drug sensitivity assays. Combined treatment with rosiglitazone and panobinostat showed synergistic effects, leading to more apoptosis and lower viability/increased cell death compared to single-agent treatments, indicating enhanced efficacy. No specific dose-response effect or comparison between high vs. low intensity/stage is detailed for panobinostat alone. CRISPR screening inherently selects for genes conferring the greatest resistance, as these clones outgrow others. No altered ROS levels were observed with different panobinostat dosages in SIRT1 modulated cells, suggesting other mechanisms for cytotoxicity.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screening was primarily performed in human B-ALL (Nalm6 cell line), specifically identifying genes that regulate sensitivity and resistance to panobinostat, focusing on its mechanism related to acetylation modification. The transcription level of SIRT1 was significantly associated with panobinostat sensitivity across diverse tumor types (N=571/576 cancer cell lines), suggesting a broader applicability of SIRT1 as a biomarker beyond ALL. The synergistic effect of rosiglitazone and panobinostat was observed across different ALL cell lines (Nalm6, REH, SEM). SIRT1's role in modulating panobinostat sensitivity was confirmed in multiple ALL cell lines (Nalm6, REH, 697, UOCB1). SIRT1 disturbing in Nalm6 cells led to resistance to other HDAC inhibitors (chidamide and vorinostat) but did not affect sensitivity to conventional chemotherapeutic agents. Panobinostat targets class I, II, and IV HDACs, with limited effects on class III HDACs (sirtuins), but SIRT1 (a class III HDAC) manipulation impacts panobinostat sensitivity, highlighting a context-dependent role and cross-talk in drug combinations.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), especially those experiencing drug resistance. Also, patients with higher SIRT1 expression in cancer cells across diverse tumor types (N=571/576 cancer cell lines). Specific ALL subtypes noted to have higher SIRT1 expression and potentially benefit from panobinostat therapy include MEF2D-rearrangement, ZNF-rearrangement, hyperdiploid, mixed-lineage leukemia gene rearrangement, and TCF3-PBX1. Infant ALL is also mentioned for sensitivity. ALL cells (Nalm6, REH, SEM, KOPN8, 697, UOCB1 cell lines) were used for in vitro studies.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Improved treatment outcomes for ALL patients by overcoming panobinostat resistance. Stratification of patients who might benefit from panobinostat treatment. The findings suggest therapeutic strategies to overcome panobinostat resistance in ALL by reactivating mitochondrial functions or modulating specific genes like SIRT1 (e.g., activating OXPHOS or mitochondrial activity, or enhancing SIRT1 activity can sensitize ALL cells to panobinostat). This provides a rational basis for panobinostat in combination with mitochondrial activators to overcome resistance.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility (SIRT1 expression as a potential biomarker for panobinostat response and patient stratification based on sensitivity/resistance). Protective/Therapeutic benefit (overcoming drug resistance, improving prognosis, sensitizing ALL cells to panobinostat, identifying strategies to enhance panobinostat efficacy). Adverse risk (related to drug resistance).

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Genome-wide unbiased CRISPR/Cas9 screening consistently revealed mitochondrial-related processes as drivers of panobinostat resistance, and its validity was confirmed by the positive selection of HDAC1. These results were corroborated by RNA-seq data, GO biological process enrichment, and experimental validation (e.g., MTT assays for PMAIP1, BAK1, SIRT1; DCFH-DA for ROS; TMRM for MMP). The functional role of mitochondrial activity was further confirmed by rosiglitazone sensitizing ALL cells to panobinostat. Correlations between gene expression (POLG, GABPA, TFB1M, SIRT1) and panobinostat sensitivity (IC50) were robustly observed across a large panel of diverse cancer cell lines (N=571/576) using public databases (DepMap, Sanger GDSC1), enhancing generalizability and reliability. Modulation of SIRT1 expression consistently affected panobinostat sensitivity and apoptosis across multiple ALL cell lines. Independent reports also confirmed SIRT1's role. While SIRT1 transcription level is presented as a 'potential biomarker' with 'significantly associated' findings, suggesting promise, further experiments from patient-derived samples and mouse models are warranted to fully consolidate these findings for routine clinical use.
